questions.question: What is an Organizational Unit (OU) in AWS Organizations?

options.text: A logical grouping of AWS accounts

explanation.correct: An OU is a logical grouping of AWS accounts within AWS Organizations — like a folder for accounts.
explanation.why: OUs are used to group accounts for easier policy management and organization.

questions.question: Which account in AWS Organizations pays the bills for all member accounts?

options.text: Each account pays its own bills separately
AWS pays all bills for organizations

explanation.correct: The management account (master account) receives and pays the consolidated bill for all member accounts.
explanation.why: Consolidated billing is a key feature of AWS Organizations — one invoice from the management account.

questions.question: What does SCP stand for in AWS Organizations?

explanation.correct: SCP stands for Service Control Policy — a JSON policy that controls what actions member accounts can or cannot perform.
explanation.why: SCPs are the primary governance tool in AWS Organizations for restricting what accounts can do.

questions.question: An SCP denying EC2 actions is attached to Dev-OU. Which users inside a Dev-OU member account are affected?

options.text: Only IAM users, not the root user
Both IAM users AND the root user

explanation.correct: SCPs apply to all users AND roles in a member account, including the root user.
explanation.why: This is a critical exam point — SCPs override even root user permissions in member accounts.

questions.question: What is a key benefit of Consolidated Billing in AWS Organizations?

options.text: Free access to all AWS services
Combined usage across accounts may qualify for volume discounts

explanation.correct: Consolidated Billing combines usage across all accounts, which can help reach volume discount tiers that no single account would hit alone.
explanation.why: This is one of the primary cost management benefits of AWS Organizations.

questions.question: AWS WAF operates at which layer of the network model?

explanation.correct: AWS WAF operates at Layer 7 (Application layer), inspecting HTTP/HTTPS request content.
explanation.why: WAF reads request content (URLs, headers, body) — this is L7 work. Shield handles L3/L4.

questions.question: Which of the following can AWS WAF be attached to?

options.text: CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway

explanation.correct: WAF can be attached to CloudFront, Application Load Balancer (ALB), Amazon API Gateway, and AWS AppSync.
explanation.why: WAF sits in front of these services to filter traffic before it reaches your backend resources.

questions.question: What does a rate-based rule in AWS WAF do?

options.text: Limits how many requests a single IP can make in a time period

explanation.correct: Rate-based rules block (or count) requests from any IP address that exceeds a defined request limit within a specified time window.
explanation.why: Rate-based rules are the primary defense against bot floods and brute-force attacks.

questions.question: What is the difference between AWS Shield Standard and AWS Shield Advanced?

options.text: Standard protects EC2, Advanced protects S3
Standard is free and automatic (L3/L4); Advanced is paid and adds L7 protection and DRT access
Standard is paid, Advanced is free
They are the same service with different names

explanation.correct: Shield Standard is free and automatically protects all AWS customers at L3/L4. Shield Advanced (~$3000/month) adds L7 protection, 24/7 DRT access, and cost reimbursement.
explanation.why: Know both tiers, their cost, and what each covers — commonly tested.

questions.question: What does DDoS stand for?

explanation.correct: DDoS stands for Distributed Denial of Service — an attack where many compromised computers flood a target with traffic to overwhelm it.
explanation.why: The 'Distributed' part means the attack comes from many sources simultaneously, making it hard to block.

questions.question: What does Amazon Inspector do?

options.text: Monitors CloudTrail for suspicious API calls
Automatically scans EC2 and containers for software vulnerabilities
Tracks configuration changes in AWS resources

explanation.correct: Amazon Inspector is an automated security assessment service that scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and network exposure.
explanation.why: Inspector = vulnerability scanning. Don't confuse with GuardDuty (threat detection) or Config (configuration compliance).

questions.question: AWS Config is best used for which of the following scenarios?

options.text: Blocking SQL injection attacks on a web application
Detecting when an S3 bucket's configuration changed from private to public
Scanning for malware on EC2 instances
Monitoring network traffic for DDoS attacks

explanation.correct: AWS Config records every configuration change and evaluates resources against compliance rules — perfect for detecting when a bucket that should be private becomes public.
explanation.why: Config is about configuration compliance and drift detection, not attack blocking or traffic monitoring.

questions.question: A GuardDuty finding shows 'CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS'. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Your EC2 instance is running a legitimate cryptocurrency exchange
An EC2 instance may be compromised and performing crypto mining
AWS is billing you for cryptocurrency usage
Your EC2 instance is DDoS-ing a crypto website

explanation.correct: This finding type indicates that an EC2 instance is querying DNS names associated with cryptocurrency mining pools — a strong indicator of compromise.
explanation.why: GuardDuty uses ML and threat intelligence to detect unusual behaviors like unauthorized crypto mining.

questions.question: Which data sources does Amazon GuardDuty automatically analyze?

options.text: Application logs, database query logs, S3 access logs
CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs
EC2 instance memory dumps and file system scans

explanation.correct: GuardDuty automatically ingests and analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs to detect threats using ML.
explanation.why: You don't need to configure log collection for GuardDuty — it handles this automatically.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of AWS Security Hub?

options.text: To aggregate and centralize security findings from multiple AWS security services
To block attacks in real time
To manage IAM users across accounts

explanation.correct: Security Hub aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Config, Macie, Access Analyzer, and third-party tools into a single centralized dashboard.
explanation.why: Security Hub is a 'single pane of glass' for security — it consolidates, doesn't replace, other services.

questions.question: IAM Access Analyzer finds that an S3 bucket is accessible from outside your zone of trust. What does this mean?

options.text: The bucket is encrypted with the wrong key
External AWS accounts or the public internet can access the bucket
The bucket is empty and needs content

explanation.correct: IAM Access Analyzer detects resources accessible outside your zone of trust (your account or organization), meaning external accounts or public internet can access them.
explanation.why: This typically means an accidental misconfiguration — bucket policy allowing public or cross-account access.

questions.question: Amazon Macie is primarily used to protect which AWS service?

explanation.correct: Amazon Macie uses ML to discover and classify sensitive data specifically in Amazon S3 buckets.
explanation.why: Macie is S3-focused. It scans S3 objects for PII, financial data, credentials, and other sensitive content.

questions.question: When should you use Amazon Detective instead of Amazon GuardDuty?

options.text: To detect threats in real time before they happen
To investigate and analyze what happened AFTER a security incident
To block malicious traffic at the network edge

explanation.correct: Detective is a post-incident forensic investigation tool — it helps you understand the root cause, timeline, and scope of a security incident after it has been detected.
explanation.why: GuardDuty detects; Detective investigates. The smoke alarm fires (GuardDuty), then the investigator arrives (Detective).

questions.question: You want to allow only traffic from India to your web application and block all other countries. Which WAF rule type achieves this?

explanation.correct: Geo-based rules in WAF allow you to allow or block traffic based on the originating country of the request.
explanation.why: Geo-based = location-based filtering. Rate-based = request frequency. IP-based = specific IPs.

questions.question: A company's S3 bucket was accidentally changed from private to public at 2 PM yesterday. They discover this at noon today. Which service would show them exactly when the change was made?

explanation.correct: AWS Config records a timeline of all configuration changes, so it would show exactly when the bucket permission changed and what the configuration was before and after.
explanation.why: Config = audit trail of configuration changes. This is its core function.

questions.question: Your organization wants to prevent all member accounts from disabling AWS CloudTrail logging, even if the root user tries. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Create an IAM policy in each account that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging
Create an SCP in AWS Organizations that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and attach it to the root of the organization
Use AWS Config to detect and auto-remediate

explanation.correct: SCPs are the only mechanism that can restrict even root users in member accounts. Creating an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and attaching it at the root OU level affects all accounts, including their root users.
explanation.why: IAM policies don't control root users. Config only detects — it doesn't prevent. SCPs prevent at the account level, even for root.

questions.question: Which combination of AWS services provides both DDoS protection AND protection from SQL injection and bot attacks?

explanation.correct: Shield protects against DDoS (volumetric network floods at L3/L4). WAF protects against application-layer attacks like SQL injection, XSS, and bots (L7). Together they cover all layers.
explanation.why: The instructor called WAF + Shield the 'best combo' — complementary coverage across all attack layers.

questions.question: A security audit finds that an IAM role in your account has a trust policy allowing any external AWS account to assume it. Which service would have detected this?

explanation.correct: IAM Access Analyzer analyzes resource-based policies (including IAM role trust policies) to detect when resources are accessible from outside your zone of trust, including external AWS accounts.
explanation.why: Access Analyzer focuses on ACCESS PATHS — who can access what. This includes role trust policies, bucket policies, KMS key policies, etc.

questions.question: In a multi-account AWS environment, which service configuration allows you to see all GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config findings from ALL accounts in one place?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail in each account and aggregate to one S3 bucket
Configure AWS Security Hub with an administrator account and member accounts
Use AWS Config aggregator without Security Hub
Create cross-account IAM roles for each security service

explanation.correct: AWS Security Hub supports multi-account configurations through AWS Organizations. You designate one account as the Security Hub administrator and all member accounts' findings are aggregated there automatically.
explanation.why: Security Hub + Organizations = centralized security visibility across all accounts in one dashboard.

questions.question: Amazon Detective pulls data from which sources to perform its investigation?

options.text: Inspector vulnerability reports and WAF logs
CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings
Config compliance reports and Macie findings
EC2 system logs and RDS query logs

explanation.correct: Amazon Detective automatically ingests CloudTrail event logs, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings to build a complete behavioral graph for investigation.
explanation.why: Detective builds on GuardDuty data — it's designed to investigate incidents that GuardDuty has already detected.

questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between SCPs and IAM permission boundaries?

options.text: SCPs apply to accounts (including root), permission boundaries apply to individual IAM entities (users/roles)
Permission boundaries apply to accounts, SCPs apply to users
Both apply to the same things in different ways
SCPs are free, permission boundaries are paid

explanation.correct: SCPs are AWS Organizations policies that apply to entire AWS accounts (including root users). Permission boundaries are IAM policies that limit the maximum permissions of individual IAM users or roles within an account.
explanation.why: Both are 'guardrails' but operate at different levels: SCPs at account level, permission boundaries at entity level.

questions.question: Which statement about AWS Shield Standard is TRUE?

options.text: It requires manual configuration for each AWS resource
It is automatically enabled at no cost for all AWS customers

explanation.correct: AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled for all AWS customers at no additional cost and provides protection against the most common network and transport layer DDoS attacks.
explanation.why: Standard = free + automatic. Advanced = paid + more features. This is a common exam distinction.

questions.question: Trusted Advisor shows a resource in RED status. What does this mean?

options.text: The resource has been automatically shut down
AWS has billed you extra for this issue
Action is recommended — AWS has identified a potential issue
The resource is permanently broken and must be deleted

explanation.correct: Red status in Trusted Advisor means 'Action Recommended' — AWS has detected a potential issue and recommends you review it. AWS never forces you to take action.
explanation.why: Even red = 'recommended' not 'required'. AWS is advisory only — you always retain control.

questions.question: Amazon Macie uses which technology to classify sensitive data in S3?

options.text: Manual scanning by AWS security engineers
Machine learning to detect patterns of sensitive data types
Hash comparison against known file signatures

explanation.correct: Amazon Macie uses machine learning (ML) to automatically discover, classify, and protect sensitive data in S3, identifying patterns that match PII, financial data, and credentials.
explanation.why: ML enables Macie to find sensitive data even in large datasets without manually reviewing every file.

questions.question: You need to host a static website using S3 and CloudFront with a custom domain. The Route 53 Alias record for the domain should point to which resource?

explanation.correct: When using CloudFront, the Route 53 Alias record should point to the CloudFront distribution domain name. The S3 bucket endpoint approach only works when the bucket name exactly matches the domain name — using CloudFront removes this restriction.
explanation.why: In class: a student's S3-direct approach failed because the bucket name didn't match the domain. CloudFront as an intermediary solves this.

questions.question: Which service would you use if you suspect files in your S3 buckets contain credit card numbers that are publicly accessible?

explanation.correct: Amazon Macie uses ML to scan S3 buckets for sensitive data like credit card numbers (PII, financial data). It will flag if that sensitive data is in a publicly accessible bucket.
explanation.why: Macie = sensitive data in S3. Credit card numbers = financial PII = exactly what Macie detects.
